cards._note: IT-01 | C A1; G9; Treccani Plurale dei nomi | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G19 (research §10)

p: Learn each noun with an article: grammatical gender is not the same as sex.

items.meaning: bread / night: -e can be either gender

gloss: The night is long.
is feminine, so
has -a.

notice: Endings are clues, not guarantees. Check the noun with its article.

cards._note: IT-31 | C A1; Treccani Plurale dei nomi | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G19 (research §10)

p: Change the noun ending and the article together.

gloss: The houses are small.

notice: Not every noun changes: learn irregular and invariant plurals with the noun.

sections.heading: Articles
sections.sub: Choose the form and the intended reference.

cards._note: IT-02 | C A1 R/B1; G1 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Match gender and number, then the sound of the next word.

items.meaning: masculine, s + consonant, z, gn, ps: the student(s)
masculine before a vowel: the friend(s)
feminine: the house(s), the female friend(s)

gloss: The student reads the book.

notice: The next word may be an adjective. Article use does not match English in every context.

cards.search: the definite articles il lo la

cards._note: IT-03 | C A1 R/B1; G1 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Use an indefinite article for one nonspecific person or thing.

example.t: Ho un amico e un’amica a Roma.

gloss: I have a male friend and a female friend in Rome.

notice: Masculine un has no apostrophe before a vowel. These articles have no plural form.

cards._note: IT-32 | C articles/quantity extension; G1,G15 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: For an unspecified amount or some countable items,
+ article can act as a partitive.

term.t: dei libri / degli amici / delle mele

example.t: Compro del pane e delle mele.

gloss: I’m buying some bread and some apples.

notice: Partitives are not compulsory everywhere. The same forms can mean of/from the.

cards._note: IT-04 | C A1/B1; G13 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; corrective source G31 (research §10): family article/modifier variation

p: The possessive agrees with what is possessed, not with the owner’s gender.

term.t: il mio / la mia / i miei / le mie

items.meaning: your (informal singular) / his or her: same ending pattern
our / your (plural) / their; the last form is invariant

gloss: His or her car is new.
agrees with
, not the owner.

notice: Normally use article + possessive. Singular family nouns have a bounded exception.

cards._note: IT-05 | C A1/B1; U quello; G1 analogy | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G21 (research §10)

p: Point to something near or further away; match the noun’s gender and number.

example.t: Questo libro è mio; quello è tuo.

gloss: This book is mine; that one is yours.

notice: Before a masculine noun,
changes like an article. Alone, use
, not

cards._note: IT-08 | C A1-B1; U; Treccani Nessuno; G14 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G24 (research §10)

p: Decide whether the word counts things, distributes them, or replaces the noun.

items.meaning: much/many / so much/many / little/few; agree before a noun

gloss: I read a few books every month.
and
stay singular here.

notice: and
take singular nouns. English “a few” does not justify a plural after

cards._note: IT-53 | U; Treccani Bello | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G21 (research §10)

p: Before a noun, masculine
follows article-like sound choices.

example.t: Ho un bel libro e dei bei quaderni.

gloss: I have a beautiful book and some beautiful notebooks.

notice: After the noun or
, use ordinary
. Most adjectives do not shorten this way.

cards._note: IT-06 | C A2; G9 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G20 (research §10)

p: An adjective describes a noun and follows its gender and number.

items.meaning: big: one singular, one plural form for both genders

gloss: The keys are small.
is feminine;
is plural.

notice: Agreement still applies after
. Some adjectives are invariant.

cards._note: IT-44 | C B1; Treccani Qualificativi aggettivi | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G20 (research §10)

p: A descriptive adjective often follows the noun; some common adjectives can precede it.

items.meaning: a red house: classifying colour after noun
an Italian film: relation/origin after noun

gloss: I met a long-standing friend.

notice: Position can change emphasis or meaning. “All Italian adjectives follow the noun” is false.

cards._note: IT-07 | C B1; U; G14 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G22 (research §10)

p: Compare a property, or distinguish “the most” from “very”.

term.t: più alto di / meno alto di

example.t: Luca è più alto di Marco.

gloss: Luca is taller than Marco.

notice: -issimo means very/extremely, not “the most in a group”. The comparison link is not always

cards._note: IT-41 | U; G14 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Many manner adverbs use an adjective’s feminine singular base + -mente.

gloss: Speak slowly, please.

notice: Before -mente, adjectives in -
/-re often drop final e. Not every English -ly word uses -mente.

cards._note: IT-42 | C A1-B1; G14; Treccani Negazione | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G24 (research §10)

p: Adverbs describe a verb, adjective or another adverb; place depends on the word and focus.

example.t: Non ho mai visto quel film.

gloss: I have never seen that film.

notice: No single position rule covers all adverbs.
can mean “ever” in a question.

sections.heading: Numbers and dates
sections.sub: Closed patterns for amounts, dates and times.

cards._note: IT-43 | C A1-A2; Treccani Numerali | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G23 (research §10)

p: Use cardinal numbers for quantities; ordinals agree with nouns.

items.meaning: It is one o’clock / two o’clock

example.t: La lezione è il primo maggio alle due.

gloss: The lesson is on the first of May at two o’clock.

notice: Dates normally use cardinals after day one. Ordinals change for gender and number.

sections.heading: Present forms
sections.sub: Regular patterns and essential irregular verbs.

cards._note: IT-09 | C A1; G3 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G29 (research §10)

p: The present can describe a habit, a current situation or an action happening now.

term.t: parlo, parli, parla; parliamo, parlate, parlano

items.meaning: speak; I, you, he/she, we, you plural, they

term.t: credo, credi, crede; crediamo, credete, credono
dormo, dormi, dorme; dormiamo, dormite, dormono
finisco, finisci, finisce; finiamo, finite, finiscono

gloss: I speak Italian and work here.

notice: Not every -ire verb uses -isc-. Italian present can translate English “am doing” without a progressive.

cards._note: IT-33 | C A1-B1 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G30 (research §10)

p: Keep frequent irregular forms together; the Italian grammatical subject controls the verb ending, even when its pronoun is omitted.

term.t: sono / sei / è / siamo / siete / sono

items.meaning: be; I / you / he-she / we / you plural / they

term.t: ho / hai / ha / abbiamo / avete / hanno

items.meaning: I go / I do-make / I come / I know how or know a fact

example.t: Ho una chiave e sono a casa.

gloss: I have a key and I am at home.

notice: An
form does not predict the whole paradigm. Modals have their own forms in the modals card.

cards._note: IT-11 | C B1; G6,G8 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Match the pronoun to the subject; many routine verbs have a pronominal form.

term.t: mi lavo / ti lavi / si lava

items.meaning: I wash myself / you wash yourself / he-she washes

term.t: ci laviamo / vi lavate / si lavano

items.meaning: we wash / you plural wash / they wash
get up / meet each other: base forms end in -si

gloss: We met each other yesterday.

notice: Not every -
verb means literally “oneself”. Personal reflexive/reciprocal compound forms use

cards.search: reflexive and reciprocal mi ti si

cards._note: IT-12 | C A1-B1; G8 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G27,G30 (research §10)

p: Put the modal before an infinitive, without adding a or

term.t: posso, puoi, può; possiamo, potete, possono

items.meaning: can: I / you / he-she / we / you plural / they

term.t: devo, devi, deve; dobbiamo, dovete, devono
voglio, vuoi, vuole; vogliamo, volete, vogliono

example.t: Non posso venire, ma voglio aiutarti.

gloss: I can’t come, but I want to help you.

notice: Do not insert the English word “to”.
+ infinitive often expresses a learned skill.

cards.search: can must want potere dovere volere

cards._note: IT-13 | C construction extension; Crusca Mi piacerebbe sapere | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G26 (research §10)

p: The liked thing is the grammatical subject; the person experiencing the liking is indirect.

items.meaning: to me / to you / to him / to her
is pleasing: I like one thing or an activity
are pleasing: I like several things

gloss: I like these books.
controls the plural verb.

notice: Do not make the experiencer an English-style subject of

cards._note: IT-14 | C A1-B1; G2,G8 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Use a present auxiliary + past participle for a past event viewed as a whole.

term.t: ho parlato / ho creduto / ho dormito
ho fatto / ho detto / ho visto

items.meaning: I did-made / said / saw: irregular participles

gloss: Yesterday I worked at home.

notice: This tense often translates English simple past. It is not limited to recent events or English “have done”.

cards._note: IT-34 | C A1-B1; U; G8 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Learn the auxiliary with the verb and construction; meaning and pronoun position can matter.

items.meaning: I left: be auxiliary + subject agreement
I finished / it finished: changed construction

example.t: Ho camminato, poi sono tornata a casa.

gloss: I walked, then I returned home (female speaker).

notice: “All motion verbs take
” is false. Some verbs and modals allow alternatives.

cards._note: IT-35 | U; G9,G10 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Check the auxiliary and the function of any preceding pronoun.

term.t: Anna è arrivata / i ragazzi sono arrivati

items.meaning: preceding feminine them: agree with object
I bought two of them: feminine items

gloss: The keys? I found them.
replaces feminine plural

notice: Not every preceding object behaves like
. Nonpartitive
does not trigger this object agreement.

cards._note: IT-15 | C A2-B1; G2 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Use the imperfect to view a past situation from inside: background, habit or an action underway.

term.t: parlavo, parlavi, parlava; parlavamo, parlavate, parlavano

items.meaning: parlare = speak: I / you / he-she / we / you plural / they
I believed / I slept or was sleeping

term.t: ero, eri, era; eravamo, eravate, erano

gloss: As a child I used to play here (male speaker).

notice: The imperfect is a viewpoint, not simply “a long action” or every English “was”.

cards._note: IT-16 | C A2-B1; U; G2,G18 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; hosts IT-52 recognition in named dialog block

p: Choose the viewpoint in context: a bounded event, or a situation viewed from inside.

items.meaning: I read the book: whole event
I used to go every summer: habit

gloss: I was reading when you called me.

notice: Duration and repetition alone do not decide the tense. Recognition:
forms are explained in Details.

cards.search: past choice event or background passato remoto

cards._note: IT-39 | U B1 supplement; G2,G8 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Use an imperfect auxiliary + participle to place an event before another past reference point.

items.meaning: we / you plural / they had done
I / you / he-she had arrived, etc. with the be auxiliary

example.t: Quando sono arrivata, il treno era già partito.

gloss: When I arrived, the train had already left (female speaker).

notice: Choose the auxiliary as for the compound past.
is useful context, not a compulsory trigger.

cards.search: earlier than a past moment trapassato prossimo

cards._note: IT-17 | U B1; G3,G4 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G29 (research §10)

p: Use a future form for a prediction or later event; a present can also express a contextualized plan.

term.t: parlerò, parlerai, parlerà; parleremo, parlerete, parleranno

items.meaning: I / you / he-she / we / you plural / they will speak
I will believe / sleep: same future endings
I will be / have / go / do

gloss: I’m leaving tomorrow; I’ll return on Monday.

notice: Distance alone does not force a tense. Future can also express a present-time guess.

cards._note: IT-18 | C B1 and A1 vorrei; U | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Use present conditional for a softened request, desire, advice or uncertainty.

term.t: parlerei, parleresti, parlerebbe; parleremmo, parlereste, parlerebbero

items.meaning: I / you / he-she / we / you plural / they would speak
I would like / could you / he-she should

gloss: Could you help me? I’d like to understand.

notice: English “would” has several uses. This card does not teach the full unreal-condition system.

cards._note: IT-19 | C A1-B1; G16 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Choose informal singular
or plural
; negative
uses the infinitive.

gloss: Take the book and read it (

notice: Positive
commands attach object pronouns. Formal
uses a different pattern.

cards._note: IT-36 | U B1; G16 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Formal singular address uses third-person present-subjunctive forms as instructions.

items.meaning: excuse me / say-tell / come: formal singular
tell me / take it: pronoun before formal command

gloss: Please tell me (formal singular address).

notice: Unlike positive
commands, formal
commands place the pronoun before the verb.

sections.heading: Subjunctive
sections.sub: Bounded B1 patterns, with recognition notes.

cards._note: IT-20 | U B1; R; G5 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; hosts IT-51 recognition in named dialog block

p: Certain constructions select a mood: begin with common opinions, wishes and necessity.

term.t: che io parli / che tu parli / che lui parli

items.meaning: that I / you / he speak: -are singular uses -i

term.t: che noi parliamo / voi parliate / loro parlino

items.meaning: that we / you plural / they speak

gloss: I hope you are well.

notice: Not every
clause takes subjunctive. Recognition:
(past subjunctive) is included in Details; full sequencing is deferred.

cards._note: IT-37 | U B1; G3 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G28 (research §10)

p: Use this construction to focus on a process underway at a particular moment.

term.t: sto / stai / sta / stiamo / state / stanno

items.meaning: present of stay/be: I / you / he-she / we / you plural / they
I was reading: imperfect of stay/be + gerund

gloss: I’m reading; I’ll call you later.

notice: The simple present can also describe what is happening now. Do not use the progressive for every English -ing.

cards._note: IT-38 | U B1; G3 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G28 (research §10)

p: Use
when an event is on the point of happening.

items.meaning: we were about to go out

example.t: Sto per uscire. Hai le chiavi?

gloss: I’m about to go out. Do you have the keys?

notice: This means imminent, not every intention expressed by English “going to”.

sections.heading: Sentence basics
sections.sub: Subjects, questions, negatives and generic statements.

cards._note: IT-10 | C A1; G6,G9,G10 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: The ending identifies the subject when context is clear; say the pronoun for emphasis or clarification.

items.meaning: you speak: formal singular / informal singular

gloss: I speak English. And you?

notice: Italian often omits a recoverable subject. Formal
still takes third-person singular verb forms.

cards.search: subjects and address io tu lei

cards._note: IT-21 | C A1-B1 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G25 (research §10)

p: A yes/no question can keep statement word order. Question words identify what you need to know.

items.meaning: how much/many: agree with a noun

gloss: How many books do you have?

notice: No English do-support or obligatory subject–verb inversion. Intonation distinguishes many spoken yes/no questions.

cards._note: IT-45 | C A1-B1; Treccani Negazione | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G24 (research §10)

p: Put
before the finite verb and any object pronouns.

items.meaning: I don’t understand / I don’t understand it

example.t: Non ho mai visto nessuno qui.

gloss: I have never seen anyone here.

notice: Negative words after the verb normally need
in negative statements. Before the verb,
can negate without

cards.search: not never nobody non mai nessuno

cards._note: IT-46 | C A2-B1 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G25 (research §10)

p: Use a short exclamatory pattern to highlight a quality or amount.

items.meaning: How lovely! / What a beautiful house!
So many books! / So many people!

gloss: What a beautiful day!

notice: stays unchanged.
changes with a following noun; punctuation and context distinguish an exclamation from a question.

cards._note: IT-30 | C A2 R; U B1; G6,G17 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Use
for an unspecified human agent: people, generic you, or sometimes we.

items.meaning: people eat well: verb used without an object
books are sold: passive construction, plural

gloss: People speak Italian in Italy.

notice: Not every
means “oneself”, and not every
construction has a singular verb.

cards._note: IT-22 | C A1 R/A2 P/B1; G6,G9 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Replace a direct object without adding a preposition; match its gender and number.

items.meaning: him-it / her-it / them masculine / them feminine
I see it / I want to see it

gloss: The keys? I’m looking for them.
replaces feminine plural

notice: A normal finite verb has the clitic before it. Infinitives and positive informal commands use attachment.

cards.search: direct objects lo la li le

cards._note: IT-23 | C A2 R/B1 P; G6,G7 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Replace a recipient or experiencer introduced by a in the verb’s pattern.

items.meaning: to me / to you / to us / to you plural
to them; explicit phrase / common modern clitic

gloss: I give her the book.
means to her here, not feminine plural them.

notice: The same spelling can serve a different function: identify the verb’s recipient versus direct object.

cards._note: IT-40 | U B1; G6,G7,G9 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: In common recipient + direct-object combinations, put the recipient first.

term.t: me / te / se / ce / ve + lo/la/li/le/ne

items.meaning: recipient/reflexive form changes before the second clitic
to him or her + it/them/of it: joined spelling
he-she gives it to me / wants to give it to me

gloss: The book? I’ll give it to him/her tomorrow.

notice: The final
identifies the direct object, not the recipient’s gender. This is a bounded common ordering pattern.

sections.heading: ci and ne
sections.sub: Recover the intended phrase, not an English word.

cards._note: IT-24 | U; G11 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

h: · us, there, or a verb pattern?

p: Recover the phrase
stands for: a person group, a place or a selected complement.

items.meaning: I think about it / I believe in it

example.t: Vai a Roma? Sì, ci vado domani.

gloss: Are you going to Rome? Yes, I’m going there tomorrow.

notice: is not one fixed English word and does not replace every prepositional phrase.

cards.search: ci us there or a verb pattern

cards._note: IT-25 | U; G11,G9 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

h: · of it, of them, about it

p: Use
for a quantity taken from an identified set, or in selected
-phrases.

items.meaning: I don’t want any of them (masculine items)
I talk about it: the pattern talk about

example.t: Quante mele vuoi? Ne voglio due.

gloss: How many apples do you want? I want two of them.

notice: Keep the quantity when it is needed.
does not always mean “some”; full idiomatic verb inventories are deferred.

cards._note: IT-26 | C A1-B1; G15 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Choose a relationship in the Italian construction, rather than one English equivalent.

items.meaning: between-among or in a future interval: alternatives

gloss: I’m going to Anna’s with Luca.

notice: Each preposition has several uses. A verb’s selected preposition may differ from English.

cards.search: simple prepositions di a da in

cards._note: IT-47 | C A1 R/A2-B1; G15 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Combine
/a/da/in/su with the definite article required by the next word.
Article order for the rows:

p.t: il / lo / l’ / la / i / gli / le

term.t: di → del / dello / dell’ / della / dei / degli / delle
a → al / allo / all’ / alla / ai / agli / alle
da → dal / dallo / dall’ / dalla / dai / dagli / dalle
in → nel / nello / nell’ / nella / nei / negli / nelle
su → sul / sullo / sull’ / sulla / sui / sugli / sulle

example.t: Il libro è nello zaino, vicino alla porta.

gloss: The book is in the backpack, near the door.

notice: Do not fuse every preposition.
usually stays separate;
also occur.
normally stay separate.

cards._note: IT-27 | C prepositions/adverbs; G15; Treccani temporal expressions | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G29 (research §10)

p: Choose the location or time relationship, then the construction’s tense.

term.t: a Roma / in Italia / da Anna

items.meaning: in-to Rome / in-to Italy / at-to Anna’s
for two years, continuing from the past

term.t: per due ore / due ore fa

items.meaning: for two hours (duration) / two hours ago
in two days / at two o’clock

gloss: I’ve lived here for two years. The situation is still continuing.

notice: Ongoing duration commonly uses Italian present + da, even when English uses a perfect tense. Place choices have lexical exceptions.

cards.search: place and duration a in da per

cards._note: IT-28 | C A1 R/A2-B1; U; G12 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Link a description to a noun: use
for a subject or direct object, preposition +
for other relations.

items.meaning: the book that I’m reading: object
the person who is speaking: subject
the person I’m talking to: prepositional relation
the house where I live: place

example.t: Questo è il libro che cerco.

gloss: This is the book I’m looking for.

notice: Do not omit
as you can omit English object “that”. Do not strand the preposition after

cards._note: IT-29 | C A1-B1; U cause/consequence | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: Select the relation between ideas before selecting a connector.

example.t: Sono stanca, quindi resto a casa.

gloss: I’m tired, so I’m staying home (female speaker).

notice: These words do not all introduce the same clause type.
can also mean “then” in time.

cards._note: IT-48 | C A1-B1; U; G5 | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G27 (research §10)

h: That, when, because, in order to

p: Choose a finite clause with a subject, or a bounded infinitive pattern.

items.meaning: I know that… / I think I will… (same subject)

example.t: Leggo per capire, perché il testo è difficile.

gloss: I read in order to understand, because the text is difficult.

notice: Cause
and purpose
need different mood choices. This card does not teach full tense backshift.

cards.search: that when because in order to

cards._note: IT-50 | C A1 R/A2; G4; Treccani Periodo ipotetico | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending

p: For a condition treated as open or real, use indicative in the
clause.

items.meaning: if you have time, call me

example.t: Se hai tempo, vieni con noi.

gloss: If you have time, come with us.

notice: Italian permits future after
. Unreal and past-counterfactual systems are deferred; do not extend this pattern to every English “if”.

sections.heading: Verb + infinitive
sections.sub: Learn the linking pattern with the verb.

cards._note: IT-49 | C infinitives/B1 complements; U di-a | sources: research/it-en-plan.md §2; authored; independent linguistic review pending; supplemental sources G27 (research §10)

p: Learn the first verb with its infinitive pattern; English “to” does not select a or

items.meaning: can / must / want: no added preposition
I think I will / hope to: same subject

example.t: Cerco di capire e comincio a scrivere.

gloss: I try to understand and start writing.

notice: These are selected patterns, not a rule that every verb takes the same link.
+ finite verb can introduce a different subject.

cards.search: verb infinitive a di no link

gender.title: Noun gender
gender.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Common exceptions
runs: refers to a male/female tourist; the article supplies the gender.

detail.label: People and agreement
comment: The person is kind.
stays feminine even when the person is a man.

detail.label: A useful habit
runs: . The noun supplies the gender; articles and adjectives respond to it.

plural.title: Noun plurals
plural.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Spelling
runs: (bank → banks): h keeps the hard sound.
(male friend → male friends): -co/-go plurals need checking; there is no safe single rule.

definite.title: The
definite.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Plural choices

runs.t: gli studenti / gli amici / le amiche

comment: the students / the male or mixed-group friends / the female friends. Feminine plural
normally remains unelided.

detail.label: Use and omission
comment: I like music. / I study Italian. Generic music has an article here; the language after
does not. Learn the construction, not “use the wherever English does”.

indefinite.title: A/an
indefinite.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Feminine elision
comment: a woman / an island. The apostrophe marks the missing -a of

detail.label: More than one
comment: I have friends in Italy. / I have some friends in Italy. Plural indefiniteness has other expressions; it is not a plural

partitive.title: Some
partitive.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Amount or relationship?

runs.t: Il colore del vino è rosso.

comment: I drink some wine. / The colour of the wine is red. Only the first
is a partitive.

detail.label: Alternatives
comment: I’m buying bread. / I’m buying a little bread. With a quantity expression, use
rather than a second partitive article.

detail.label: Negation and questions
comment: I’m not buying bread. / Would you like some bread? Do not translate English any mechanically; a negative statement often has a bare noun.

possessives.title: My/his/her
possessives.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Family nouns

runs.t: mia sorella / le mie sorelle / il loro padre

comment: my sister / my sisters / their father. Plain singular family terms commonly omit the article, but plurals and
retain it.

detail.label: Family nouns with modifiers

runs.t: la mia sorellina / la mia cara sorella

comment: my little sister / my dear sister. Use the article with diminutives and adjectives before the family noun. Following modifiers vary:

comment.t: mio fratello maggiore / mio fratello gemello

comment: (my older brother / my twin brother) are allowed without it;
(my twin brother) is also possible. Some combinations require it, such as
(my favourite female cousin). Article choice after the noun can depend on the expression, meaning or register.

detail.label: Without the noun

runs.t: La tua casa è grande; la mia è piccola.

comment: Your house is big; mine is small.
replaces
and retains its feminine singular form.

detail.label: Predicative ownership
comment: This book is mine. After
in this ownership construction, the possessive can appear without an article.

demonstratives.title: This/that
demonstratives.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Feminine forms
comment: that house / that female friend / those houses. Feminine plural is

detail.label: With and without a noun

runs.t: Quei libri sono nuovi; quelli sono vecchi.

comment: Those books are new; those ones are old. The independent pronoun is

detail.label: Intervening adjective
comment: that good student / that student. The following sound decides the shortened form.

bello.title: Beautiful
bello.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Position changes the form

runs.t: bei libri / libri belli / i libri sono belli

comment: beautiful books / beautiful books / the books are beautiful.

detail.label: Feminine vowel
comment: a beautiful female friend / some beautiful female friends. Feminine plural stays

detail.label: Next word
comment: a beautiful new book / a beautiful show. Match the next word, not a distant noun; check unfamiliar loanword sounds in a dictionary.

agreement.title: Adjective agreement
agreement.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Two classes

runs.t: un libro interessante / una casa interessante / case interessanti

comment: an interesting book / an interesting house / interesting houses. -e becomes -i regardless of gender.

detail.label: Across the verb

runs.t: La casa è nuova; i libri sono nuovi.

comment: The house is new; the books are new.

detail.label: Bounded exceptions

runs.t: una maglia rosa / due maglie rosa

comment: a pink sweater / two pink sweaters.
used as a colour adjective stays unchanged. Do not add -s as in an English plural noun.

position.title: Adjective position
position.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: A meaning contrast

runs.t: una certa notizia / una notizia certa

comment: some particular news / certain (reliable) news. The interpretation depends on position and context.

detail.label: Not arbitrary
comment: an interesting Italian film. A relation adjective such as
normally follows the noun.

detail.label: Useful default
runs: Start with noun + descriptive adjective. Learn common pre-noun combinations as phrases, rather than moving every English adjective to the same side.

comparison.title: Comparisons
comparison.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Choosing the comparison link

runs.t: Luca è più alto di me.
È più facile leggere che scrivere.

comment: Luca is taller than me. / Reading is easier than writing.
compares these two infinitives; do not replace every than with

detail.label: Equality

runs.t: Luca è tanto alto quanto Marco.

comment: Luca is as tall as Marco. Both patterns express equality;
are unchanged here because they modify an adjective.

detail.label: Relative and absolute

runs.t: È il più alto della classe.

comment: He is the tallest in the class. / He is very tall. Add gender/number endings:

detail.label: Irregular forms
comment: This book is better. / People eat better here.
describes a noun;
modifies how an action happens.
give
also have
in some meanings.

indefinites.title: All, some, each, none
indefinites.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Agreement

runs.t: molta acqua / molti libri / tutte le case

comment: much water / many books / all the houses. Used as adverbs,
do not agree:
= I work a lot.

detail.label: Individuals
comment: Each person has a key. / I have no book.
is singular.
follow the indefinite-article shape before a noun.

detail.label: Replacing a noun
comment: Someone is arriving. / I’m looking for something new.
and
take a singular verb;
describes something new, not something again.

detail.label: Negative position
comment: Nobody is coming. In these statements, a negative word before the verb removes
; after the verb it needs

mente.title: Forming manner adverbs
mente.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: The base
comment: clear → feminine clear → clearly. The resulting adverb does not change for gender or number.

detail.label: Shortened bases
comment: easy → easily / particular → particularly. Learn the derived form with its meaning.

detail.label: Useful non-mente forms
comment: well / badly / a lot. These frequent adverbs have their own forms. An English adjective/adverb label does not determine an Italian suffix.

adverb-use.title: Using time, place and quantity words
adverb-use.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Adjective or adverb
comment: It is a good book. / He/she writes well.
describes the noun;
describes the action.

detail.label: Typical placement
comment: I have already eaten. / I often go there.
often sits between auxiliary and participle; place expressions often follow the verb.

detail.label: Meaning changes with context
comment: Have you ever been to Rome? / I never go to Rome.

detail.label: Quantity
comment: many houses / very beautiful (feminine plural). The adjective
agrees with
; the degree adverb
stays unchanged.

numbers-dates.title: Numbers, dates and clock time
numbers-dates.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

runs.t: undici, dodici, tredici, quattordici, quindici, sedici, diciassette, diciotto, diciannove, venti

comment: eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty.

detail.label: Larger cardinals

runs.t: trenta / quaranta / cinquanta / sessanta / settanta / ottanta / novanta / cento / mille

comment: thirty / forty / fifty / sixty / seventy / eighty / ninety / a hundred / a thousand.
= 28: drop the tens’ final vowel before
= 23 has a written accent.

detail.label: Ordinals

runs.t: quarto, quinto, sesto, settimo, ottavo, nono, decimo

comment: fourth through tenth. Above ten, usually base minus final vowel +
= eleventh; use
= twenty-third.
= the second lesson.

detail.label: Dates and times

runs.t: il due maggio / alle tre e mezza / alle quattro meno un quarto

comment: on the second of May / at half past three / at quarter to four.
is singular;
and later clock hours are plural.

detail.label: Counting objects

runs.t: un libro / una casa / due libri / due case

comment: one book / one house / two books / two houses.
has gender/article-like variants before a noun; other simple cardinals such as
are invariant.

present.title: Present tense
present.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Read the endings
runs: to find the stem, then use the person ending.
comment: you work / we work. A written subject is unnecessary when the context identifies it.

detail.label: Spelling

runs.t: cerco → cerchi / pagare → paghi / mangiare → mangi

comment: I look for → you look for / to pay → you pay / to eat → you eat. -care/-gare keep the hard sound with h; not every spelling retains all infinitive letters.

detail.label: Now or habitual
comment: What are you doing? I’m reading. / I read every evening. Use
to focus explicitly on an ongoing process, not for every present sentence.

irregulars.title: Essential irregulars
irregulars.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Go — forms
comment: I go / you go / he-she goes / we go / you plural go / they go.

detail.label: Do/make — forms
comment: Present forms of do/make, in the same person order.

detail.label: Come — forms
comment: Present forms of come, in the same person order.

detail.label: Give — forms
comment: Present forms of give.
(gives) has an accent;
(from) does not.

detail.label: Stay/be — forms
comment: Present forms of stay;
also helps form the progressive.

detail.label: Drink — forms
comment: Present forms of drink.

detail.label: Say/tell — forms
comment: Present forms of say/tell.

detail.label: Know — forms
comment: Knowing facts or knowing how:
= I can swim (have the skill).
is used for familiarity:
= I know Rome.

reflexives.title: Reflexive and reciprocal
reflexives.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Routine
comment: I get up at seven. / I have to get up early. Attach the pronoun to an infinitive after dropping final e.

detail.label: Reciprocal meaning
comment: Anna and Luca greet each other. The context identifies a reciprocal action, rather than each greeting themselves.

detail.label: Past agreement

runs.t: Anna si è alzata; Marco si è alzato.

comment: Anna got up; Marco got up. In these personal patterns, the participle follows the subject’s gender and number.

detail.label: Not always literal
comment: My name is Anna. Learn
as a pattern; a literal “I call myself” translation is not needed here.

modals.title: Can, must, want
modals.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Meaning
comment: I have to leave. / I want to leave. / May I leave?
can concern permission or possibility, depending on context.

detail.label: Pronoun alternatives
comment: I want to see it/him. Both placements are possible; do not use both pronouns together.

detail.label: Past forms
comment: I had to work. / I had to go out (female speaker). Auxiliary choice and accepted alternatives are explained under Auxiliary choice.

piacere.title: I like…
piacere.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: One item or activity
comment: I like the film. / I like reading. An infinitive subject takes singular

detail.label: Named experiencer

runs.t: A Luca piacciono i film italiani.

comment: Luca likes Italian films.
identifies who likes them, not the subject controlling

detail.label: Past
comment: I liked the lesson. / I liked the books. Use
; agree with
(feminine singular) or
(masculine plural).

compound-past.title: Completed past
compound-past.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Build the form
comment: I bought a book. / We left yesterday (male or mixed group). Auxiliary is present; the participle carries the lexical action.

detail.label: Common irregular participles

runs.t: essere → stato; fare → fatto; dire → detto; vedere → visto; leggere → letto; scrivere → scritto; prendere → preso; venire → venuto; bere → bevuto

comment: be → been; do → done; say → said; see → seen; read → read; write → written; take → taken; come → come; drink → drunk. Choose the auxiliary separately.

detail.label: Negation
comment: I didn’t understand.
precedes the auxiliary; do not add English did.

detail.label: Whole event

runs.t: Ho abitato qui per dieci anni.

comment: I lived here for ten years. A long but bounded period can still use
; length alone does not demand

auxiliary.title: Auxiliary choice
auxiliary.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Object versus event
comment: I started the work. / The work started. Transitive active use takes
; this intransitive use takes

detail.label: Modals
comment: I had to leave. / I had to work. Modals often follow the infinitive’s auxiliary;
can also occur with an intransitive infinitive, as in

detail.label: Reflexive placement with a modal
comment: I had to get up (female speaker in the first example). With the clitic before the modal, use
; attached to the infinitive, use
in this pattern.

detail.label: A limit
comment: I wanted to be present. A modal before the infinitive
uses
. Look up unfamiliar intransitive constructions rather than inventing a motion rule.

participle-agreement.title: Past-participle agreement
participle-agreement.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: The ordinary pattern
comment: I saw her/it (feminine). / I saw them (masculine or mixed).
can elide to
; the participle still identifies gender.

detail.label: Combined objects
comment: The letters? I gave them to him/her.
follows feminine plural letters, not the recipient.

detail.label: First- and second-person variation
comment: Maria, I saw you. Both invariable and agreeing participles occur with these preceding direct-object pronouns; do not mark one automatically wrong.

detail.label: Partitive versus topic

runs.t: Di mele ne ho comprate tre.
Di quel problema ne ho parlato.

comment: I bought three apples. / I talked about that problem. The first
is partitive; the second means about it and does not cause agreement. More complex quantified
cases are outside this slice.

imperfect.title: Past background
imperfect.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Other regular patterns

runs.t: credevo, credevi, credeva, credevamo, credevate, credevano
dormivo, dormivi, dormiva, dormivamo, dormivate, dormivano

comment: Imperfect of believe and sleep in the six-person order shown on the card.

detail.label: Have — forms

runs.t: avevo, avevi, aveva, avevamo, avevate, avevano

comment: I had / you had / he-she had / we had / you plural had / they had.

detail.label: Background and interruption
comment: It was raining when I went out. The rain is background; the departure advances the narrative.

detail.label: Frequent stems
comment: I was doing / saying / drinking. Irregular infinitives
use
before imperfect endings.

detail.label: Habits
comment: Every summer we used to go to the seaside. A repeated situation without a bounded summary is a normal imperfect use.

past-choice.title: Past choice
past-choice.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: A bounded repetition
comment: I called three times. / I used to call every evening. Counted, bounded repetition can use the compound past.

detail.label: A long event

runs.t: Ho lavorato lì per dieci anni.
Lavoravo lì quando ci siamo conosciuti.

comment: I worked there for ten years. / I was working there when we met. The first summarizes a bounded period; the second sets background.

detail.label: Changed viewpoint with modals

runs.t: Potevo uscire, ma sono rimasto a casa.

comment: I could go out, but stayed home. / I was able to go out. The compound past commonly presents the realized opportunity; context still matters.

detail.label: Knowing versus finding out
comment: I knew the answer. / I found out the news yesterday. English “knew” cannot be substituted mechanically.

detail.label: Recognition: narrative simple past

runs.t: fu ← essere; disse ← dire; andò ← andare; fece ← fare

comment: he/she was; said; went; did/made. These are bounded-event past forms, frequent in narrative and with regional contemporary uses. They are not solely literary, and distance in years alone does not select the tense. Productive paradigms are deferred.

pluperfect.title: Earlier than a past moment
pluperfect.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Have auxiliary pattern

runs.t: Avevo già letto il libro quando è uscito il film.

comment: I had already read the book when the film came out. The reading is earlier than the film’s release.

detail.label: Be auxiliary and agreement
comment: We had left before eight (all-female group). The participle agrees as in

detail.label: Do not add it everywhere

runs.t: Ieri ho letto e poi ho dormito.

comment: Yesterday I read and then slept. A simple sequence can use two compound past forms; not every past narrative needs a pluperfect.

future.title: Future reference
future.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Regular and spelling patterns

runs.t: credere → crederò; dormire → dormirò; cercare → cercherò; pagare → pagherò; mangiare → mangerò

comment: I will believe / sleep / look for / pay / eat. -are changes to -er- in the normal pattern; h preserves the hard sound.

detail.label: Essential irregular stems

runs.t: essere → sar-; avere → avr-; andare → andr-; fare → far-; venire → verr-; potere → potr-; dovere → dovr-; volere → vorr-; sapere → sapr-; bere → berr-; dire → dir-; stare → star-

comment: Add the future endings to these stems:
= he/she will come;
= they will be able to.

detail.label: Inference
comment: Where is Anna? She’s probably at home.
need not describe a later time.

detail.label: After if
comment: If he/she comes, we’ll talk. Italian can use a future after
; the English restriction after if does not transfer.

conditional.title: Polite requests and advice
conditional.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Forms

runs.t: farei / andrei / verrei / dovrei / potrei / vorrei

comment: I would do / go / come / should / could / would like. Check the double r in
and

detail.label: Advice and desire
comment: You should rest. / I would like to leave.

detail.label: Uncertainty
comment: It could be true. This expresses a possibility rather than a polite request.

detail.label: A1 recognition
comment: I’d like a coffee, please. This useful formula can be recognized before mastering the whole conditional.

imperative.title: Commands to tu/voi
imperative.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Useful irregulars

runs.t: sii / siate; abbi / abbiate; vieni / venite; di’ / dite

comment: be; have; come; say:
is the singular command of

detail.label: Short commands

runs.t: fa’ / fai; va’ / vai; da’ / dai; sta’ / stai

comment: do, go, give, stay (
). The short forms use an apostrophe, not an accent.

detail.label: Attachment
comment: give me / tell me / make-let me / tell him. With the shortened commands, most following initial consonants double;
does not.

detail.label: Negative alternatives
comment: Don’t do it (
, two placements). / Don’t do it (
). The pronoun may precede or follow in these negative commands.

formal-command.title: Formal singular instructions
formal-command.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Compare address
comment: Tell me! (
) / Please tell me! (
). Both request the same action, with different address and placement.

detail.label: Positive and negative
comment: Please come in. / Do not come in here. Formal negatives retain the finite form, unlike negative

detail.label: Useful forms
comment: be / have / do / go, addressed to
. These come from the present subjunctive.

detail.label: A shared invitation
comment: Let’s go! / Let’s not forget the keys. The
invitation is included here as a bounded related pattern.

present-subjunctive.title: Present subjunctive
present-subjunctive.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Regular forms

runs.t: parli, parli, parli, parliamo, parliate, parlino
creda, creda, creda, crediamo, crediate, credano
dorma, dorma, dorma, dormiamo, dormiate, dormano

comment: Speak / believe / sleep:
adds -isc- in the same four persons as its present indicative.

detail.label: Essential irregulars

runs.t: sia, sia, sia, siamo, siate, siano
abbia, abbia, abbia, abbiamo, abbiate, abbiano

comment: Present subjunctive of
(be) and
(have), in the same person order. Other common singulars:
(go),
(do),
(come),
(can),
(must),
(want),
(know),
(stay/be).

detail.label: Frequent triggers and a contrast
comment: I think it is useful. / I want you to come. / It is necessary for us to leave. / I know it is useful.
asserting a fact takes indicative here.

detail.label: Same subject
comment: I think I’ll leave. / I think Anna will leave. The same-subject infinitive often avoids a finite mood choice; it does not justify removing
whenever subjects differ.

detail.label: Two connector patterns
comment: I speak slowly so that you understand. / Although it is late, I’m staying. Purpose
differs from causal
selects subjunctive. Full connector taxonomy is deferred.

detail.label: Register
runs: (I think/believe that), indicative occurs in informal speech. Use the subjunctive as the standard learner pattern here; do not describe every informal indicative as meaningless or every

detail.label: Recognition: past subjunctive
comment: I think he has left. / I believe he/she has finished.
+ participle marks an earlier, completed event relative to this present belief. Recognize the construction and agreement; productive tense sequencing is outside this slice.

progressive.title: Ongoing action
progressive.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Current versus habitual
comment: I am working now. / I work every day. A habitual statement normally uses the ordinary present.

detail.label: Past viewpoint
comment: I was cooking when you arrived (male addressee). The action was underway at the reference moment.

detail.label: Irregular gerunds

runs.t: fare → facendo / dire → dicendo / bere → bevendo

comment: do → doing / say → saying / drink → drinking.

detail.label: English mismatch
comment: I like reading. The activity after
is an infinitive, not a gerund just because English uses -ing.

about-to.title: About to
about-to.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Two constructions
comment: I am about to read. / I am reading.
+ infinitive precedes the start; the gerund focuses on the ongoing process.

detail.label: Imminence in the past

runs.t: Stavo per telefonarti quando hai chiamato.

comment: I was about to phone you when you called. This does not assert that the planned call actually took place.

detail.label: A scheduled plan
comment: Next year I’m studying in Italy. A future-reference present can express a plan without implying it is about to happen.

subjects.title: Subjects and address
subjects.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: When a pronoun helps
comment: I’m staying; you’re leaving. Pronouns highlight the contrast rather than fill an obligatory English subject slot.

detail.label: Third person

runs.t: Lui lavora; lei studia; loro abitano qui.

comment: He works; she studies; they live here.
are ordinary contemporary subject forms.

detail.label: Formal address
comment: Are you ready, Mr Rossi? / Are you ready, Ms Rossi? Formal
uses a third-person verb; the adjective normally matches the person addressed.

detail.label: No dummy it
comment: It’s raining. / It’s late. Do not insert an English-style dummy subject pronoun.

questions.title: Questions
questions.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Yes/no
comment: Do you have time? / Do you have time? (with explicit focus or clarification on you).

detail.label: Which
comment: Which book do you want? / Which books do you want?
has no masculine/feminine distinction.

detail.label: Agreement
comment: How much water do you want? / How many apples do you want?

detail.label: What and who
comment: Who is coming? / What are you reading?
as the subject of this ordinary question takes a singular verb.

negation.title: Not, never, nobody
negation.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Before and after
comment: Nobody is coming. Both are negative; Italian negative concord is not the English “two negatives make a positive” rule.

detail.label: Nothing and no longer
comment: I see nothing. / I no longer work here.

detail.label: Compound tense
comment: I didn’t see him/it. / I have never been there (female speaker).
precedes the clitic and auxiliary;
normally follows the auxiliary.

detail.label: A question is different
comment: Have you ever seen this film?
does not mean never in every question. The negative-statement rule is not a universal ban on postverbal negative words without

exclamations.title: What a…! How…!
exclamations.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: No extra indefinite article
comment: What a beautiful book! In this pattern Italian does not insert
after

detail.label: Number and gender
comment: What beautiful houses! / So many houses!
stays the same; the adjective
and quantifier
agree with case.

detail.label: Question contrast
comment: How many books do you have? / So many books! The first asks for information; the second expresses a reaction.

direct.title: Direct objects
direct.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Position
comment: I see him/it. / I want to see him/it. / Look at him/it! Drop final e from
before attaching

detail.label: Strong forms
comment: They called me, not you. / Come with me. Strong
express contrast or follow a preposition.

detail.label: Past
comment: The letter? I read it.
can elide before
still agrees with

detail.label: Verb function
comment: I’m waiting for Anna. I’m waiting for her.
has a direct object even though English uses for; check the Italian verb pattern.

indirect.title: Indirect objects
indirect.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Named recipient
comment: I phone Luca. I phone him.
takes an indirect recipient in Italian, despite English phone him.

detail.label: Strong and weak
comment: I give the book to her (explicit or contrasted recipient). / I give her the book.

detail.label: Plural and register

runs.t: Ho dato il libro a loro.

comment: I gave the book to them. Plural
is common in contemporary usage;
is explicit. Formal written
after the verb also occurs:
(I gave them the book).

detail.label: Two spellings, two jobs
comment: I see them (feminine direct objects). / I write to her (indirect recipient). Do not infer the function solely from the pronoun’s spelling.

ci.title: The place and complement particle
ci.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Existence

runs.t: C’è un libro; ci sono due chiavi.

comment: There is a book; there are two keys. Singular/plural follows what exists.

detail.label: Selected patterns

runs.t: Tengo a questo progetto. Ci tengo.

comment: I care about this project. I care about it. / I try to do it. I try. Learn
with their meaning; the particle is not an interchangeable English preposition.

detail.label: Place and people

runs.t: Conosciamo Roma e ci torniamo spesso.

comment: We know Rome and often return there. / Anna calls us. Only the first
is a place replacement.

detail.label: Two different particles
comment: I think about the problem: I think about it. / I talk about the problem: I talk about it. The Italian regency, not the English word about, selects the particle.

ne.title: The quantity and topic particle
ne.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Quantity including zero

runs.t: Hai libri italiani? Sì, ne ho tre.

comment: Do you have Italian books? Yes, I have three of them. / I have none.
keeps the already-known set recoverable.

detail.label: Topic

runs.t: Parliamo del viaggio. Ne parliamo domani.

comment: We’re talking about the trip. We’ll talk about it tomorrow.
replaces
+ the topic.

detail.label: Past agreement

runs.t: Di mele ne ho comprate due.
Di libri ne ho comprati due.

comment: I bought two apples. / I bought two books. In these ordinary quantified patterns, agree with the items counted.

detail.label: Position and accent

runs.t: Non voglio né tè né caffè.

comment: I want to take two of them. / I want neither tea nor coffee. Attach
to the infinitive; accented
connects negatives and is a different word.

combined.title: Two pronouns
combined.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Fusion

runs.t: Le do il libro. Glielo do.
Gli do le chiavi. Gliele do.

comment: I give her the book. I give it to her. / I give him the keys. I give them to him. Both
and
become
in these combinations.

detail.label: Position
comment: I can give it to you (two placements). / Give it to me! Keep the combination together; informal commands attach it.

detail.label: Elision and agreement
comment: The letter? I gave it to him/her.
can elide;
agrees with
, not the recipient.

detail.label: Adding the quantity particle

runs.t: Di libri? Me ne dà due.

comment: Books? He/she gives me two of them. The first clitic changes to
before
too. Full multi-clitic strings and idiomatic meanings are outside this card.

impersonal-si.title: Generic people
impersonal-si.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Generic human subject
comment: People work a lot here. / We’re leaving tomorrow (in an appropriate shared-plan context).

detail.label: Passive-si agreement
comment: A house is for sale. / Houses are for sale. In the passive pattern,
controls singular/plural; the seller is unspecified.

detail.label: Personal reflexive versus impersonal

runs.t: Qui ci si lava prima di entrare.

comment: Luca washes himself. / Here people wash themselves before entering.
avoids a sequence of two
forms.

detail.label: Boundary
runs: This card covers ordinary present patterns. The compound impersonal-
agreement system and every possible ambiguous
construction are deferred; do not extrapolate “

contracted.title: Preposition + the
contracted.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Select the article first
comment: to the student / in the backpacks. The next sound affects the article and therefore the contraction.

detail.label: Vowel and number

runs.t: dell’amica / delle amiche / all’amico / agli amici

comment: of the female friend / of the female friends / to the male friend / to the male or mixed-group friends.

detail.label: Separate forms

runs.t: con il libro / col libro / per gli amici

comment: with the book (two accepted forms) / for the friends. Do not invent
fusion as the normal learner form.

detail.label: Two jobs of del

runs.t: del pane / il prezzo del pane

comment: some bread / the price of the bread. The first is a partitive; the second expresses
+ definite article.

time-place.title: Place and duration
time-place.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Ongoing versus bounded
comment: I’ve been studying Italian for a year (and still do). / I studied for an hour.
locates the start of a continuing situation;
measures a duration.

detail.label: Since and ago
comment: I’ve lived here since 2020. / I arrived two hours ago (male speaker).
can take a date, not only an amount of time.

detail.label: Destination/location

runs.t: Sono a casa. Vado a casa.
Sono in ufficio. Vado in ufficio.

comment: I’m at home. I’m going home. / I’m in the office. I’m going to the office. The same preposition can serve position and destination.

detail.label: Bounded place phrases

runs.t: al mare / in montagna / dal medico / a destra / vicino a casa

comment: at-to the seaside / in-to the mountains / at-to the doctor / on-to the right / near home. Learn the construction rather than deriving it solely from English in or to.

relatives.title: Relative clauses
relatives.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: No gender change

runs.t: la ragazza che parla / i ragazzi che parlano

comment: the girl who speaks / the boys who speak.
is invariant; the verb still agrees with its subject.

detail.label: Choose the preposition

runs.t: il problema di cui parliamo / la persona a cui scrivo

comment: the problem we are talking about / the person I’m writing to. The relation comes from

detail.label: Recognition

runs.t: gli amici con i quali viaggio

comment: the friends with whom I travel.
are agreeing relative forms, especially useful in formal clarity; productive complex relatives are deferred.

detail.label: Place

runs.t: la città in cui vivo / la città dove vivo

comment: the city where I live: two choices. Do not extend
to every time or abstract relation.

connectors.title: Add, contrast, explain, conclude
connectors.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Contrast
comment: I’m staying; Luca, on the other hand, is leaving.
contrasts the two choices.

detail.label: Explanation

runs.t: Resto a casa: infatti sono stanca.

comment: I’m staying home: in fact, I’m tired.
supports the preceding statement;
introduces its consequence.

detail.label: Correlation

runs.t: Non solo legge, ma anche scrive.

comment: He/she not only reads but also writes. Keep the two linked parts parallel.

detail.label: Cause versus consequence
comment: I’m staying because it’s raining. / It’s raining, so I’m staying. A cause clause and a conclusion have different jobs.

subordinates.title: That, when, because, in order to
subordinates.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Finite and infinitival complements
comment: I know Anna is leaving. / I think I’ll leave. The infinitive has the same understood subject as
in this pattern; a different subject normally needs a finite clause.

detail.label: Time
comment: When you arrive, call me. / While I read, I take notes. Italian may use future after
when the intended time is future.

detail.label: Before an action

runs.t: Prima di uscire, chiudo la porta.

comment: Before going out, I close the door. The same person closes the door and goes out; use
+ infinitive for this bounded pattern.

detail.label: Cause and purpose
comment: I speak slowly because I am tired (male speaker). / I speak slowly so that you understand. The purpose clause uses subjunctive;
+ infinitive expresses a same-subject purpose.

verb-infinitive.title: Verb + infinitive
verb-infinitive.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: No link
comment: I want to leave. / I like reading. Neither construction inserts a or

detail.label: Linking with the first pattern
comment: I’m learning to swim. / I keep reading. Learn
and
as complete patterns.

detail.label: Linking with the second pattern
comment: I finish working. / I decide to leave. Italian infinitives can correspond to English -ing forms.

detail.label: Subject contrast
comment: I hope to arrive soon. / I hope Anna arrives soon. The finite different-subject clause needs its own person and mood.

real-conditions.title: Real/open if
real-conditions.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Present or future

runs.t: Se domani piove, resto a casa.
Se domani pioverà, resterò a casa.

comment: If it rains tomorrow, I’ll stay home. Both can express an open future condition; choice depends on how the speaker frames it.

detail.label: A consequence can be a command
comment: If you arrive early, wait for me. The main clause can give an instruction.

detail.label: Boundary
runs: A remote or contrary-to-fact hypothesis uses other tense/mood combinations. A past English would or had does not license copying this real-condition pattern; that system is outside this slice.

lookup-help.title: How to use this reference
lookup-help.lead: Find the decision, check the form, then open its limits.

detail.label: Four views
runs: Forms: nouns, articles and agreement. Verbs: conjugation, past choices and mood. Sentences: questions, negatives and pronouns. Links: prepositions and clauses.

detail.label: Meaning support
runs: Each Italian sentence has an English meaning. A form inventory names its person order or function; auxiliary forms explain the construction rather than force word-for-word translation.

detail.label: Levels and boundary
runs: This is a selective A1–B1 lookup, not a full course or exam syllabus. B1 supplementary topics have bounded depth. Past subjunctive and narrative
are recognition notes, not full production targets.

detail.label: Search and dialogs
runs: Search in English or use visible Italian forms, such as
. Search filters cards; Details contains contrasts and exceptions. Clear search to return to your selected view.

simple-prepositions.title: Simple prepositions
simple-prepositions.lead: Check the forms, then compare the situations and limits.

detail.label: Relationship

runs.t: il libro di Anna / un regalo per Anna / parlo con Anna

comment: Anna’s book / a gift for Anna / I talk with Anna. These are different relationships, not interchangeable labels.

detail.label: Person and destination
comment: I’m going to Rome. / to Italy. / to the doctor.
can express a destination associated with a person.

detail.label: Other relations
comment: The book is on the table. / A book about Rome.
can indicate location or topic.

detail.label: Verb pattern
comment: I’m trying to understand. / I’m starting to understand. Learn
with the governing verb; there is no universal translation of to.
